cells.tense: You are paying attention to what comes back, right now, and it is coming back even.
cells.ask: Name one exchange that has stayed even, and tell the other person out loud that it has.
cells.core:
You're keeping the scales level without making a project of it. Somebody does for you, you do for them, and the returns land about where they should. That evenness takes endurance in the body — you can hold it a long while because you're not secretly keeping score.

The body notices this. You give because giving feels right, not because you're owed, and you can take what's offered without a flinch. That's the harvest arriving where it should: in your hands and theirs, about the same.

Where the balance gets tested is when you're tired and the exchange keeps asking. The way to keep it alive is one more honest turn: tell someone the thing has stayed fair. What you name, you get to hold.
cells.sheetLine: You give and take evenly, and you can hold it steady.
cells.verb: keeping the exchange even, give and take still squaring up
cells.place: in the body's long haul, where things have to be held for the duration

cells.tense: You are bracing for the moment the scales tip, ahead of it, before anyone has reached for anything.
cells.ask: Pick one exchange you are tracking closely. Step back from it for a day and let the other person settle their side.
cells.core:
You're carrying the fairness for both sides of the exchange. Before the tab is open, you've already priced it — who owes what, what you'll need to give, what you'll get back — and you hold the whole ledger in your own hands. Underneath the alertness is endurance doing work nobody asked for.

The bookkeeping costs the thing it's protecting. Fairness doesn't need a watcher. When you brace, the other person can feel the grip, and giving starts to feel like a transaction with a deadline. The weight you're carrying is mostly the load of watching.

You don't have to put the scales down forever. Just long enough to see what happens when you let a turn go unmeasured. What holds up will hold up on its own, and you'll know more about the exchange than the ledger could tell you. You've got the endurance to carry it either way.
cells.sheetLine: You are carrying the fairness of both sides at once.
cells.verb: keeping the exchange even, give and take still squaring up
cells.place: in the body's long haul, where things have to be held for the duration

cells.tense: You stopped reaching for the exchange, and you are still standing where you left it.
cells.ask: Make one small fair trade today — the kind that ends when both hands are empty.
cells.core:
The exchanging stopped somewhere, and from where you stand it doesn't look like it stopped. You watch other people trade and call it, you notice what comes back for them, and you stay where you are. Something about the last exchange left you not wanting another one.

What's low isn't your ability to give or take. It's the give itself, gone quiet. The door stayed shut long enough that neither side of it gets any practice, and a thing you don't practice starts to feel less possible. That's the smallness right now — not a verdict on you.

You don't have to reopen everything. One small exchange, finished today. Start small enough that nothing much turns on it. The movement is what your side is waiting for, not the result, and the same strength is still there for you to use.
cells.sheetLine: The exchange has gone quiet, not the self that could make it.
cells.verb: keeping the exchange even, give and take still squaring up
cells.place: in the body's long haul, where things have to be held for the duration

cells.tense: The scale in you is still reading true, and the room you are reading it in does not know.
cells.ask: Say to one person, plainly: "I saw this and I said so." Pick the small one. Small is what makes it a test you can pass.
cells.core:
The answer arrives finished, whole, before you've laid out a single reason for it. Then you spend the next stretch building the case for something you saw first, and by the time you speak, your account has moved what you saw a few steps back from where it started.

What comes out of the exchange is usually fair. You do right by people, and you don't need thanks for it. The part you don't claim is that you saw it a step earlier than anyone else in the room. You call it practical, or nothing at all.

Naming one thing you saw before the reasons existed puts the pen back in your hand. That one move is what the exchange has been waiting for.
cells.sheetLine: You saw first, and you called it ordinary.
cells.verb: keeping the exchange even, give and take still squaring up
cells.place: in the body's long haul, where things have to be held for the duration

attempts.check: The one claim the record does not support is any specific history in the Too Little cell — I locate a door behind the person and must not say who stood there, when, or what it cost. The reader could reasonably object that giving and receiving unevenly is sometimes just circumstance, not a spent capacity; the ask survives that because it is one exchange finished today, useful even if the diagnosis is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line implying their life runs this way everywhere, so every claim here stays inside one thing: one give, one take, one finish.
